item.title: World War I
item.description: A teenager shot an archduke in June. By August the trains of five empires were carrying millions to a war the generals swore would end by Christmas. Gavrilo Princip was nineteen and had already missed his chance. The motorcade carrying Archduke Franz Ferdinand had sped past after another conspirator's bomb bounced off the car and wounded bystanders. Then, on June 28, 1914, the Archduke's driver took a wrong turn onto Franz Josef Street in Sarajevo, realized his error, and stopped to reverse. Princip was standing a few feet away outside a delicatessen. He fired twice. The heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne and his wife Sophie were both dead within minutes.

item.title: The Global Struggle for Women's Suffrage
item.description: New Zealand gave women the vote in 1893. Switzerland waited until 1971. One canton held out until 1990. A federal court forced it. On July 19, 1848, three hundred people crowded into the Wesleyan Chapel at Seneca Falls, New York. Elizabeth Cady Stanton read aloud a document modeled on the Declaration of Independence. It listed eighteen grievances. The ninth: "He has compelled her, if married, to be in the law civilly dead." The twelfth: "He has denied to her this inalienable right, the elective franchise." Sixty-eight women and thirty-two men signed it. The Seneca Falls Convention produced no law, no vote, no immediate change. It produced a sentence: "We hold these truths to be self-evident: that all men and women are created equal."

item.title: The Pentagon Papers and Watergate
item.description: A third-rate burglary and a leaked war history put the newspapers against a president. The president resigned. On June 13, 1971, The New York Times published the first installment of a 7,000-page classified Defense Department study of American decision-making in Vietnam. Robert McNamara had commissioned the study in 1967; it documented that four administrations had misled the public about the war. Daniel Ellsberg, a former Pentagon and RAND analyst who had helped write it, photocopied the volumes over months and passed them to the Times. Attorney General John Mitchell obtained a federal restraining order after three installments, the first prior restraint on a newspaper in American history. The Washington Post picked up the story and was enjoined too. On June 30, 1971, the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 in New York Times Co. v. United States that the government had not met the heavy burden required to censor publication. The presses ran that night.

item.title: The Vietnam War
item.description: The Vietnamese call it the American War, the third foreign army they expelled in thirty years. On August 4, 1964, the destroyer USS Maddox reported a second torpedo attack by North Vietnamese patrol boats in the Gulf of Tonkin. President Johnson went on television that evening to announce retaliatory airstrikes. Three days later, Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution 504-2, authorizing the president to use military force without a declaration of war. The first attack, on August 2, was real. The second never happened. NSA documents declassified in 2005 confirmed that the signals intelligence had been misread: sonar operators tracked their own ship's propeller wake. Johnson knew within days. He escalated anyway. On a recorded phone call with Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara, Johnson said: "I don't think it's worth fighting for and I don't think we can get out." He sent 184,000 troops by December 1965.

item.title: The Treaty of Waitangi and the New Zealand Wars
item.description: Two texts, two languages, two meanings; the treaty said 'sovereignty' in English and 'governance' in Maori. On the morning of February 6, 1840, approximately 500 Maori chiefs gathered at the house of the British Resident, James Busby, at Waitangi in the Bay of Islands. Captain William Hobson, representing the British Crown, presented a document that he said would protect Maori rights while establishing British authority over New Zealand. The missionary Henry Williams and his son Edward translated the text into Te Reo Maori overnight. By the end of the day, 43 chiefs had signed. Over the following months, the treaty was carried around the country; eventually, over 500 chiefs signed. Some refused. Some were never asked.

item.title: The Transatlantic Slave Trade
item.description: 12.5 million people crossed the Atlantic in chains. Lloyd's of London insured the ships. Barclays Bank financed the voyages. Between approximately 1500 and 1870, European ships transported an estimated 12.5 million enslaved Africans across the Atlantic Ocean to the Americas. The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database, compiled by David Eltis and David Richardson at Emory University, has documented 36,000 individual voyages. Of the 12.5 million who embarked, approximately 10.7 million survived the crossing, the Middle Passage. The remaining 1.8 million died at sea of disease, dehydration, suicide, and violence.

item.title: The Trail of Tears
item.description: A republic that declared all men equal marched 60,000 people off their land at gunpoint. On May 28, 1830, President Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act, authorizing the federal government to negotiate treaties exchanging Native lands east of the Mississippi for territory in present-day Oklahoma. The word "negotiate" was a legal fiction. The act gave the president power to override any tribe that refused, and the treaties that followed were signed under duress, by unrepresentative factions, or at the point of a bayonet.

item.title: Tiananmen Square, 1989
item.description: A man stood in front of a column of tanks, and then he disappeared. On the morning of June 5, 1989, a man in a white shirt carrying two shopping bags walked into the middle of Chang'an Avenue and stopped in front of a column of Type 59 tanks leaving Tiananmen Square. The lead tank tried to drive around him. He sidestepped to block it. The tank stopped. He climbed onto the turret, spoke to the crew, climbed down, and resumed blocking. After several minutes, two figures pulled him away. No one has confirmed his identity. The Chinese government has never acknowledged the encounter. The photograph, taken by Jeff Widener of the Associated Press from a sixth-floor balcony of the Beijing Hotel 800 meters away, became the most reproduced image of the 20th century's final decade. Inside China, it does not exist.

item.title: The Protestant Reformation
item.description: A monk nailed 95 complaints to a door, and a machine turned them into a schism no army could recall. On October 31, 1517, an Augustinian friar and professor named Martin Luther sent 95 theses against the sale of indulgences to the Archbishop of Mainz, and, by tradition, posted them on the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg. The door was the university's notice board. The theses were in Latin, addressed to scholars, an invitation to an academic debate about whether a piece of paper signed by a papal commissioner could shorten a soul's time in purgatory.

item.title: The Holocaust
item.description: IBM sold the machines that sorted people by ancestry. The trains ran on time. On January 20, 1942, fifteen men sat around a table in a villa on the Wannsee lake outside Berlin. The meeting lasted 90 minutes. SS-Obergruppenfuhrer Reinhard Heydrich chaired; Adolf Eichmann took the minutes. The agenda was the "Final Solution of the Jewish Question." The minutes, one of 30 copies, listed the Jewish population of every European country (11 million total) and outlined a continent-wide deportation program. The word "killing" did not appear. The language was bureaucratic: "evacuation," "natural diminution," "treated accordingly." Eight of the fifteen attendees held doctorates.

item.title: The Crusades
item.description: The Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople, a Christian city, instead of liberating Jerusalem. On November 27, 1095, Pope Urban II stood before a crowd at the Council of Clermont in central France and called on Christendom to march east. The Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, he declared, was in the hands of the Seljuk Turks. The crowd's response, "Deus vult!" ("God wills it!"), launched two centuries of war across three continents.

item.title: The Taiping Rebellion
item.description: A man failed the civil service exam four times. He declared himself the Son of God. 30 million people died. Hong Xiuquan sat for the Confucian imperial examination in Canton four times (1828, 1836, 1837, and 1843) and failed each time. After his second failure, he received a set of Christian missionary tracts written by Liang Afa, a Chinese convert working with the American Baptist missionary Issachar Jacox Roberts. Hong set them aside. After his fourth failure, he reread the tracts, experienced a series of visions, and concluded that he was the younger brother of Jesus Christ, sent by God to destroy demon worship in China. The Confucian establishment that had rejected him became the demonic order he was called to overthrow.

item.title: The Sykes-Picot Agreement
item.description: Two diplomats drew a line through a desert neither had walked, and a century of borders followed. In December 1915, Sir Mark Sykes stood before the British War Committee, put his finger on a map, and said he wanted to draw a line "from the 'e' in Acre to the last 'k' in Kirkuk." He was thirty-six. He had traveled the region as a tourist and an amateur, and he was about to help decide the fate of provinces holding several million people. Lord Kitchener corrected the geography. The line stayed.

item.title: The Suez Crisis
item.description: The week Britain and France discovered they were no longer empires. On July 19, 1956, John Foster Dulles withdrew the American offer to finance Egypt's Aswan High Dam. Seven days later, in a two-hour speech to a crowd in Alexandria, Gamal Abdel Nasser said the name "de Lesseps." It was a signal. As he spoke, Egyptian officers were seizing the offices of the Compagnie Universelle du Canal Maritime de Suez, the Anglo-French company that had run the canal since 1869. Nasser announced that the waterway, dug through Egyptian soil by Egyptian labor, now belonged to Egypt. The tolls would build the dam the Americans had refused to fund.

item.title: The 1918 Influenza Pandemic
item.description: It killed more people than the war it traveled on, and it was never Spanish. In the first week of March 1918, a mess cook reported to the camp infirmary at Camp Funston, Kansas, with a fever. By noon the surgeon had more than a hundred men on cots. Within three weeks, 1,100 soldiers at the camp were too sick to stand. It looked like ordinary influenza. Most of the men recovered. Then they shipped out to France.

item.title: The Spanish Civil War
item.description: A dress rehearsal for a world war, fought with borrowed planes and rewritten history. On July 17, 1936, the garrisons of Spanish Morocco rose against the Republic. General Francisco Franco flew from the Canary Islands to take command of the Army of Africa the next day. Within a week the coup had half succeeded and half failed: the plotters held Seville, Burgos, and much of the rural west and north, but workers and loyal security forces crushed the rising in Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia, and Bilbao. A country of 25 million was cut in two. What the generals expected to finish in days lasted nearly three years.

item.title: The Collapse of the Soviet Union
item.description: A lawyer, a physicist, and a construction chief signed three pages at a hunting lodge. A country of 290 million stopped existing. On the evening of December 25, 1991, Mikhail Gorbachev sat before a television camera in the Kremlin and read for twelve minutes. "Due to the situation which has evolved as a result of the formation of the Commonwealth of Independent States, I hereby discontinue my activities at the post of President of the U.S.S.R." He signed a decree transferring control of the Soviet nuclear arsenal, roughly 27,000 warheads, to Boris Yeltsin, the president of a country called Russia that had existed as an independent state for four months. At 7:32 p.m. the red flag with hammer and sickle came down over the Senate dome. The Russian tricolor went up. There was no ceremony. A caretaker did it.

item.title: The Six-Day War
item.description: Israel struck first at 7:45 a.m. By noon most of Egypt's air force was burning on the runway. At 7:45 a.m. on June 5, 1967, roughly 180 Israeli jets crossed the Mediterranean below Egyptian radar, banked south, and struck eleven airfields at once. Within three hours about 300 of Egypt's 420 combat aircraft were burning on the ground. The pilots who were supposed to defend Cairo never left the tarmac. Israel called it Operation Focus. The war was decided before most of the Arab world knew it had begun.

item.title: The Silk Road
item.description: A Roman woman wore Chinese silk without either empire knowing the other existed. In 138 BCE, Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty sent Zhang Qian westward with 100 men to find the Yuezhi people and forge an alliance against the Xiongnu nomads who raided China's northern frontier. Zhang Qian was captured by the Xiongnu within a year. He lived among them for ten years, married a Xiongnu woman, had a son, and escaped. He reached the Ferghana Valley, crossed into Bactria, and returned to Chang'an in 125 BCE (13 years after his departure) with only one of his original companions. He had failed in his diplomatic mission. He had opened the Silk Road.

item.title: September 11 and the War on Terror
item.description: Nineteen men with box cutters turned the world's most powerful military against two countries that didn't attack it. At 8:46 AM Eastern on September 11, 2001, American Airlines Flight 11 struck the North Tower of the World Trade Center. Seventeen minutes later, United Airlines Flight 175 hit the South Tower. At 9:37, American Airlines Flight 77 struck the Pentagon. At 10:03, United Airlines Flight 93 crashed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Its passengers had stormed the cockpit after learning by phone what had happened in New York. The South Tower collapsed at 9:59. The North Tower followed at 10:28. 2,977 people died: 2,753 in New York, 184 at the Pentagon, 40 in Pennsylvania.

item.title: The Scramble for Africa
item.description: Fourteen nations carved a continent in a Berlin conference room, without inviting a single African. On November 15, 1884, representatives of fourteen nations (Germany, France, Britain, Portugal, Spain, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark, Sweden-Norway, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, Russia, and the United States) gathered at Otto von Bismarck's official residence in Berlin to settle European claims to African territory. No African ruler, diplomat, or representative was present. Over 104 days, the Berlin Conference established the rules by which European powers could claim African land: "effective occupation" (meaning a flag, a garrison, and the establishment of administrative authority) superseded prior claims based on exploration or treaty.

item.title: The Rwandan Genocide
item.description: A Belgian census card from 1933 told the killers which neighbors to kill. On the evening of April 6, 1994, a surface-to-air missile struck the Falcon 50 jet carrying Rwandan President Juvenal Habyarimana and Burundian President Cyprien Ntaryamira as it approached Kigali International Airport. Both men died. Within one hour, roadblocks manned by the Interahamwe militia and Presidential Guard appeared across Kigali. Lists of names (Tutsi political figures, moderate Hutu officials, journalists, human rights workers) had been prepared in advance. The killing was not spontaneous. It was planned.

item.title: The Russian Revolution
item.description: The Tsar abdicated on a Thursday. By Friday, two governments claimed to rule Russia. By October, neither did. On the morning of February 23, 1917 (March 8, New Style), women textile workers in the Vyborg district of Petrograd walked off their jobs. It was International Women's Day. Bread lines had stretched around blocks for weeks: the capital received only half its normal grain supply that winter. By afternoon, 100,000 workers had joined the strike. By February 25, the city was paralyzed. Tsar Nicholas II, at his military headquarters in Mogilev 400 miles away, telegraphed the Petrograd garrison commander: "I order that the disorders in the capital shall be ended tomorrow." The troops opened fire on February 26, killing approximately 40 demonstrators on Nevsky Prospect. On February 27, the Volynsky Regiment mutinied. 70,000 soldiers joined the crowds within 24 hours.

item.title: The Rise of Islam
item.description: A merchant in a cave. Within 100 years, his followers had absorbed two empires. In 610 CE, a 40-year-old merchant from the Quraysh tribe of Mecca retreated to a cave on Mount Hira. According to Islamic tradition, the angel Jibril (Gabriel) appeared to him and commanded: "Read." Muhammad ibn Abdullah could not read. item.title: The Partition of India

item.title: The Opium Wars
item.description: Britain went to war twice to force a sovereign nation to buy drugs. item.title: The Mughal Empire
item.description: Twenty followers joined Akbar's new religion; his empire held a quarter of world GDP. item.title: The Mongol Conquest of Baghdad
item.description: The Tigris ran black with ink, and then it ran red. On February 10, 1258, Hulagu Khan's army breached the walls of Baghdad and began killing. The last Abbasid caliph, al-Musta'sim bi-llah, had refused Hulagu's demand to surrender and dismantle his fortifications. item.title: The Meiji Restoration
item.description: In 1853, four American warships forced open a country that had been closed for 220 years. Thirty years later, it had a constitution, a conscript army, and a rail network. On January 3, 1868, samurai from the Satsuma, Choshu, Tosa, and Hizen domains seized the gates of the Imperial Palace in Kyoto and declared the "restoration" of imperial rule. The fifteen-year-old Emperor Meiji (born Mutsuhito, enthroned six weeks earlier after his father's sudden death) issued a decree abolishing the 265-year-old Tokugawa shogunate. The last shogun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, had formally surrendered his authority two months before, but his forces fought on. The Boshin War lasted sixteen months. item.title: The Industrial Revolution
item.description: A Bengali weaver earned more than his English counterpart in 1750. By 1830, the looms of Dacca were silent. In 1712, Thomas Newcomen installed a steam-powered pump at a coal mine in Dudley Castle, Staffordshire. It burned coal to pump water out of a coal mine, a machine feeding on the substance it was built to extract. For six decades, the Newcomen engine remained a crude, fuel-hungry device confined to the pithead. Then, in 1769, James Watt (an instrument maker at the University of Glasgow who had been asked to repair a model Newcomen engine) patented a separate condenser that reduced fuel consumption by 75%. By 1784, Watt and his business partner Matthew Boulton had developed a rotary steam engine that could drive machinery. The first Boulton & Watt engine was installed in a cotton spinning mill in Papplewick, Nottinghamshire, in 1785. Within twenty years, steam power had replaced water wheels in hundreds of British factories.

item.title: The Atomic Bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
item.description: At 8:15 a.m. on August 6, a watch in Hiroshima stopped. It is still stopped. At 8:15 a.m. on August 6, 1945, the B-29 Superfortress Enola Gay, piloted by Colonel Paul Tibbets, released an uranium-235 gun-type bomb codenamed "Little Boy" over the city of Hiroshima. The weapon detonated at approximately 1,900 feet above Shima Surgical Clinic, 800 feet southeast of the intended aiming point, the Aioi Bridge. The yield was approximately 15 kilotons of TNT. The fireball reached temperatures exceeding 1 million degrees Celsius at its center. Within one second, everything within a half-mile radius was vaporized or carbonized. The blast wave, traveling at 984 feet per second, leveled 69% of Hiroshima's buildings. Of the city's 350,000 residents and military personnel, between 70,000 and 80,000 died instantly. By December 1945, the total reached an estimated 140,000.

item.title: The Haitian Revolution
item.description: Dessalines tore the white from the French tricolor. The remaining blue and red became the flag of the world's first Black republic. By the end of September, 1,000 white colonists were dead and the most profitable colony in the Western Hemisphere was producing ash instead of sugar.

item.title: The Gutenberg Revolution
item.description: A bankrupt goldsmith copied a Buddhist idea and accidentally ended the Catholic Church's monopoly on truth. Johannes Gutenberg did not invent printing. The Chinese had been printing with carved woodblocks since the 9th century. Bi Sheng created movable ceramic type around 1040, during the Song Dynasty. Korean printers cast the first metal movable type in the 1230s; the Jikji, printed in 1377, is the oldest surviving metal-type book. What Gutenberg invented, around 1440 in Mainz, was a system: an alloy of lead, tin, and antimony that could be cast into durable reusable type; an oil-based ink that adhered to metal (water-based inks, used for woodblocks, slid off); and a wooden press adapted from the screw presses used in Rhine Valley winemaking. The individual components existed. The combination did not.

item.title: The Great Depression
item.description: In 1929 America had never been richer. Four years later one in four workers had no job and nobody could agree why. item.title: The 2008 Global Financial Crisis
item.description: A bank that survived the Civil War, two world wars, and the Great Depression died on a Monday, and the credit that runs the planet froze within the week. The bankruptcy petition was filed in a Manhattan federal court at 1:45 on the morning of September 15, 2008. Lehman Brothers, founded in 1850, having survived the Civil War, two world wars, and the Great Depression, listed 639 billion dollars in assets and 619 billion dollars in debt. It was the largest bankruptcy filing in United States history. By the time markets opened in Asia, the short-term credit that moves through the global economy every day had begun to freeze.

item.title: The French Revolution
item.description: They beheaded the king in January 1793. By July 1794 they were beheading the men who had beheaded the king. On July 14, 1789, a crowd of approximately 1,000 Parisians stormed the Bastille, a royal fortress and prison in eastern Paris. The garrison of 82 invalides (retired soldiers) and 32 Swiss Guards surrendered after four hours. The crowd killed the governor, Bernard-Rene de Launay, and paraded his head on a pike through the streets. The Bastille held only seven prisoners (four forgers, two lunatics, and a dissolute young nobleman), but its fall became the revolution's founding act: the moment when the people of Paris physically dismantled the architecture of royal authority.

item.title: The Fall of Tenochtitlan
item.description: Cortés had 500 soldiers. Tenochtitlan had 300,000 people. Smallpox decided the math. Hernán Cortés burned his ships at Veracruz in August 1519. Or scuttled them; the accounts vary, but the result was the same: 500 Spanish soldiers, 16 horses, and a handful of cannons had no way home. They marched inland toward a city none of them had seen, guided by reports from coastal peoples who described Tenochtitlan as larger than any city in Spain. It was. Built on an island in Lake Texcoco, connected to the mainland by three causeways, the Aztec capital held between 200,000 and 300,000 people. Seville, the largest city in Spain, had 60,000.

item.title: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
item.description: The last emperor was a teenager. The man who deposed him sent the crown to Constantinople. On September 4, 476 CE, a Germanic military commander named Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus, the sixteen-year-old Western Roman Emperor, at Ravenna. There was no battle. No siege. No sack. Odoacer's soldiers (foederati, Germanic troops serving under Roman command) had demanded one-third of Italy's land. When the boy emperor's father, the general Orestes, refused, Odoacer killed Orestes at Piacenza on August 28 and marched on Ravenna. Romulus surrendered without resistance. Odoacer did not execute him. He granted the teenager a pension of 6,000 solidi per year and sent him to live in a villa in Campania, possibly the former palace of Lucullus on the Bay of Naples.

item.title: The Fall of Constantinople
item.description: A 21-year-old sultan, a Hungarian cannon maker turned away by the emperor who couldn't pay him, and a gate someone forgot to lock. On April 2, 1453, Mehmed II arrived before the walls of Constantinople with an army estimated between 80,000 and 200,000 men, 69 cannon, and a fleet of 126 ships. Inside the walls, Emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos commanded roughly 7,000 defenders: 5,000 Greeks and 2,000 foreign volunteers, including 700 Genoese under Giovanni Giustiniani. The city that had once held 500,000 people now sheltered fewer than 50,000.

item.title: The Fall of the Berlin Wall
item.description: A spokesman read from a note card he had not been briefed on. By midnight, the crowd at Bornholmer Strasse was walking through. On the evening of November 9, 1989, Gunter Schabowski, a member of the East German Politburo, held a press conference to announce new travel regulations. At 6:53 p.m., Italian journalist Riccardo Ehrman asked when the new rules would take effect. Schabowski shuffled through his notes, found no answer, and improvised: "As far as I know, it takes effect immediately, without delay." He had not been briefed that the regulations were supposed to take effect the following day, with orderly processing at checkpoints.

item.title: The Cyrus Cylinder
item.description: The Shah handed a replica to the UN in 1971 and called it the first bill of rights. The cuneiform on it describes a conquest. On October 12, 539 BCE, the Persian army entered Babylon without a battle. The Nabonidus Chronicle (a Babylonian cuneiform tablet now in the British Museum) records that Cyrus's general Ugbaru led troops into the city "without fighting." Nabonidus, the last Babylonian king, had already fled. Seventeen days later, on October 29, Cyrus himself entered and, according to the chronicle, "green branches were spread before him." The priests of Marduk, Babylon's patron god, had apparently decided that the Persian conqueror was preferable to their own king.

item.title: The Cuban Revolution
item.description: A failed barracks raid became the government that outlasted the Soviet Union that subsidised it. On July 26, 1953, about 135 young men attacked the Moncada barracks in Santiago de Cuba, the second largest army garrison in the country. The plan was to seize the weapons and spark a national uprising against Fulgencio Batista, who had cancelled the 1952 elections in a bloodless coup rather than lose them. The attack collapsed within minutes. More than half the attackers were captured; many were tortured and executed. Fidel Castro, a 26-year-old lawyer, was tried and given the floor to defend himself. He spoke for nearly four hours and closed with a line that outlived the regime that jailed him: "Condemn me, it does not matter. History will absolve me."

item.title: The Cuban Missile Crisis
item.description: For thirteen days, one Soviet submarine officer was the only thing between humanity and nuclear war. On October 14, 1962, a U-2 reconnaissance aircraft piloted by Major Richard Heyser photographed Soviet medium-range ballistic missile installations under construction near San Cristobal, Cuba. The SS-4 missiles, once operational, could reach Washington, D.C. in thirteen minutes. President Kennedy was briefed on the morning of October 16. He convened a group of fourteen advisors (later known as the Executive Committee of the National Security Council, or ExComm) and gave them one instruction: find a way to get the missiles out.

item.title: The Creation of Israel and the Nakba
item.description: Ben-Gurion read the declaration at 4 p.m. Eleven minutes later Washington recognised the state. By the end of the war, 700,000 Palestinians had left villages that no longer had names. item.title: The Congo Wars
item.description: The deadliest conflict since 1945 killed 5.4 million people. Most of the world cannot name the country where it happened. On October 18, 1996, the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL) crossed from Rwanda into eastern Zaire. Laurent-Desire Kabila led them, a rebel who had been fighting since the 1960s, who had once hosted Che Guevara in the mountains above Lake Tanganyika and been dismissed by Guevara as lacking "revolutionary seriousness." Behind Kabila stood the Rwandan Patriotic Army under Paul Kagame, the Ugandan People's Defence Force under Yoweri Museveni, and the Angolan army. Their stated target: the Interahamwe genocidaires who had fled Rwanda after the 1994 genocide and reconstituted in refugee camps across eastern Zaire. Mobutu Sese Seko, who had ruled Zaire for 32 years, renamed the country, the river, and himself, sent his army to stop them. His soldiers looted Kisangani instead of defending it. Kabila entered Kinshasa on May 17, 1997. Mobutu fled to Morocco, where he died of prostate cancer on September 7. Kabila renamed the country the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

item.title: The Congo Free State
item.description: Leopold II never set foot in the Congo, but his rubber quotas cost 10 million hands, lives, and futures. In 1904, a Congolese man named Nsala sat on a mission veranda in the Nsongo district and stared at a small hand and foot laid on the ground before him. They belonged to his five-year-old daughter, Boali. Soldiers of the Anglo-Belgian India Rubber Company had killed her and his wife, Boali's mother, when his village failed to meet its rubber quota. The missionary Alice Seeley Harris photographed Nsala gazing at what remained of his daughter. That photograph, reproduced in pamphlets, lantern slide lectures, and newspapers across Europe and America, became the image that forced a king to surrender a colony.

item.title: Columbus and the Columbian Exchange
item.description: Columbus carried 17 ships on his second voyage. On them were horses, cattle, pigs, and smallpox. Within 50 years, 90% of the people he'd found were dead. October 12, 1492. Columbus waded ashore on an island the Taino called Guanahani. He planted a flag, claimed the land for Ferdinand and Isabella, and wrote in his Diario that the people who greeted him, who brought food, water, and parrots, "would make fine servants" and "could easily be made Christians." He took six Taino by force before he left. On his second voyage in 1493, he brought 17 ships, 1,200 men, horses, cattle, sheep, pigs, chickens, sugar cane, wheat, and every pathogen the Old World had spent millennia cultivating. Hispaniola's Taino population (between 250,000 and 300,000 when Columbus arrived) was fewer than 500 by 1548, according to Bartolome de las Casas, who counted them.

item.title: The American Civil Rights Movement
item.description: Four college students sat at a lunch counter in Greensboro. Within two months, sit-ins had spread to 54 cities. On December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks refused to surrender her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama. She was not the first (Claudette Colvin had done the same nine months earlier, at fifteen), but Parks was the secretary of the local NAACP chapter, and the organization was ready. The Montgomery Bus Boycott lasted 381 days. Black residents carpooled, walked miles to work, and organized a parallel transportation system that cost the city bus line 65% of its revenue. On November 13, 1956, the Supreme Court ruled in Browder v. Gayle that segregated buses were unconstitutional.

item.title: The Chinese Cultural Revolution
item.description: Students beat their teachers to death with the textbooks they'd been taught from. On May 16, 1966, the Chinese Communist Party's Central Committee issued Circular 516, drafted under Mao Zedong's direction. It accused Party leadership of harboring "counter-revolutionary revisionists" who planned to restore capitalism. The circular called on the masses to identify and destroy these enemies. Within weeks, students at Tsinghua University Middle School formed the first Red Guard unit. By August, millions of teenagers wearing red armbands and carrying Mao's Little Red Book were beating their teachers, ransacking homes, and destroying temples, libraries, and ancestral shrines. Mao reviewed over 11 million Red Guards in eight mass rallies at Tiananmen Square between August and November 1966.

item.title: The Chinese Civil War and the Founding of the People's Republic
item.description: A peasant army walked out of the mountains and built the country now shaping the century. On April 12, 1927, in Shanghai, gunmen of the Green Gang and soldiers loyal to Chiang Kai-shek moved through the workers' districts before dawn. Union halls were surrounded. Between 5,000 and 10,000 Communists, labor organizers, and suspected sympathizers were shot, beheaded, or thrown into the Huangpu River within days. The First United Front between the Nationalists (Kuomintang) and the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), which had helped reunify much of China only months earlier, was finished. The two parties would fight, on and off, for the next 22 years.

item.title: The Chernobyl Disaster
item.description: A reactor exploded in Soviet Ukraine, and the world learned about it from a Swedish shoe scanner. At 1:23:40 a.m. on April 26, 1986, operators at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant in Soviet Ukraine pressed the AZ-5 emergency shutdown button on Reactor No. 4. They were running a safety test, a rehearsal for how the reactor would keep its cooling pumps running during a blackout. The test had been delayed for hours and taken over by a night shift that had not planned it. When the control rods began to lower, a design flaw in the RBMK reactor briefly spiked the power instead of cutting it. Within seconds the core exceeded 100 times its rated output.

item.title: The Bolivarian Revolutions
item.description: Bolivar went to Haiti after his defeat, got ships and soldiers from a Black republic in exchange for a promise to free the enslaved. Then he broke the promise. On July 5, 1811, the Congress of Venezuela declared independence from Spain. By July 1812, the republic was finished. An earthquake on March 26, 1812, centered on Caracas and killing an estimated 10,000 people, destroyed the patriot strongholds while leaving royalist cities intact. The Catholic clergy declared the earthquake divine punishment for rebellion. Simon Bolivar, a 28-year-old creole aristocrat who had inherited copper mines, cacao plantations, and enslaved laborers, escaped to Cartagena. He wrote a manifesto. He raised a new army. He invaded Venezuela from the west. He won. He lost again. He fled to Jamaica. He wrote another manifesto. He fled to Haiti, where Alexandre Petion, the president of the southern republic, gave him 7 ships, 250 soldiers, weapons, ammunition, and a printing press, in exchange for a single condition: abolish slavery.

item.title: The Bandung Conference
item.description: Twenty-nine nations sent delegates to a city in Java. They represented 1.5 billion people, and twenty-three of them had not been independent before 1945. item.title: The Assassination of Julius Caesar
item.description: The Senate voted him dictator for life. Forty days later, twenty-three senators voted with knives. On March 15, 44 BCE, the Ides of March, Gaius Julius Caesar entered the Senate meeting at the Theatre of Pompey in Rome. He had been declared dictator perpetuo, dictator in perpetuity, by the Senate forty days earlier. As he took his seat, Senator Tillius Cimber approached with a petition. When Caesar waved him away, Cimber grabbed his toga and pulled it from his shoulder: the signal. Publius Servilius Casca struck first, stabbing Caesar in the neck from behind. Caesar seized Casca's arm and stabbed him with his stylus. Then the others closed in: Gaius Cassius Longinus, Decimus Brutus, Marcus Brutus, and at least nineteen more. Ancient sources record 23 wounds. The physician Antistius later determined that only one (the second stab, between the ribs) was fatal. Caesar fell at the base of Pompey's statue, bleeding onto the marble floor of a building named for the man he had defeated in civil war four years earlier.

item.title: Ashoka and the Maurya Empire
item.description: A king carved his guilt into rock for everyone to read. In 261 BCE, Ashoka Maurya's army rolled through Kalinga (a kingdom on India's eastern coast, roughly modern Odisha) and killed 100,000 people. Another 150,000 were deported. These are not external estimates. Ashoka carved the numbers himself onto Rock Edict XIII, a massive stone inscription erected across his empire: "A hundred and fifty thousand people were deported, a hundred thousand were killed, and many times that number perished."

item.title: The Armenian Genocide
item.description: A Polish lawyer invented a word in 1944 to describe what happened in 1915. The word was genocide. On the night of April 24, 1915, Ottoman authorities in Constantinople arrested 235 Armenian intellectuals, clergy, physicians, editors, lawyers, and community leaders. By the end of May, the number detained reached 600. Most were deported to Chankiri and Ayash in central Anatolia. Almost none survived. The date, April 24, is commemorated annually by Armenians worldwide as Genocide Remembrance Day.

item.title: The Arab Spring
item.description: A fruit vendor set himself on fire in a town of 40,000. Three presidents fell in 281 days. On December 17, 2010, in Sidi Bouzid, a town of 40,000 in central Tunisia, a 26-year-old fruit vendor named Mohamed Bouazizi pushed his cart to its usual spot outside the governor's office. A municipal inspector named Faida Hamdi confiscated his cart and his electronic scale, his only assets, worth roughly $200. Witnesses said she slapped him. He went to the governor's office to complain. They refused to see him. At 11:30 a.m., he stood in front of the building, doused himself with paint thinner, and struck a match. He was taken to a hospital in Sfax. He died on January 4, 2011. He was 26.

item.title: Apartheid and Its End
item.description: They imprisoned him for 27 years. Then they asked him to run the country. On May 26, 1948, the Herenigde Nasionale Party won 70 seats in South Africa's general election: fewer votes than Jan Smuts's United Party, but more seats, thanks to rural constituency weighting that overrepresented Afrikaner farming districts. D.F. Malan became prime minister. Within two years, Parliament passed the Population Registration Act (classifying every South African into one of four racial groups), the Group Areas Act (designating where each group could live), and the Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act. The architecture of apartheid was not improvised. It was legislative, systematic, and indexed.

item.title: The Khmer Empire
item.description: A laser pulse through the Cambodian canopy in 2012 found a city of a million people that the jungle had hidden for 600 years. In 2012, an aircraft mounted with LIDAR equipment flew over the Cambodian jungle canopy north of Siem Reap. The laser pulses stripped away 600 years of forest growth and revealed the outlines of a city that dwarfed medieval London. Greater Angkor stretched across 1,000+ square kilometers -- an integrated network of temples, reservoirs, canals, roads, and residential mounds that had supported 750,000 or more people. No pre-industrial city on Earth had been this large. The hydraulic engineers of the Khmer Empire had built a water management system so extensive that the West Baray alone -- one of several reservoirs -- held 53 million cubic meters of water. The system fed multiple rice harvests per year for six centuries.

item.title: The Algerian War of Independence
item.description: For 37 years France would not call it a war. It named it one in 1999. At three in the morning on November 1, 1954, All Saints' Day, roughly 30 coordinated attacks struck police posts, barracks, and farms across Algeria. Seven people died. From Cairo, a radio broadcast announced a new organization, the National Liberation Front, and demanded the restoration of a sovereign Algerian state. The French Interior Minister, Francois Mitterrand, answered within days: Algeria is France, and the only negotiation is war.

item.title: The Conquests of Alexander
item.description: He named 20 cities after himself and one after his horse. In the spring of 334 BCE, Alexander III of Macedon crossed the Hellespont with 37,000 troops and 1.5 million pounds of debt. His father Philip II had been assassinated two years earlier, and several Greek city-states had revolted. Alexander razed Thebes (6,000 killed, 30,000 enslaved) and the revolts stopped.
